km-eat-43.name: Browar Księży Młyn
km-eat-43.cuisine: Craft brewpub — modern Polish/European, wood-fired pizza
km-eat-43.description: The district's namesake brewpub, brewing on-site since 2014 inside the raw red brick of Grohman's former cotton-scutching mill — exposed brickwork, a long bar and gleaming brew tanks on show. A relaxed post-industrial pub where a short seasonal menu is paired with the house lagers; a signature touch is the beetroot cream soup poured tableside from a glass bottle.
signature_dishes: House craft beers — pils, wheat, citrus IPA + rotating seasonal

km-eat-57.name: Cesky Film — Restaurant & Pub
km-eat-57.cuisine: Czech — traditional recipes + monthly seasonal menu; beer pub
km-eat-57.description: Łódź's only dedicated Czech restaurant, tucked into the former Scheibler factory complex on Księży Młyn. Playful and cinematic — walls of Czech-history photos and the animated mole Krtek screening while you eat, a nod to film that pairs neatly with the district's Museum of Cinematography. Five taps of Černá Hora and a monthly-rotating menu keep regulars coming; weekend reservations are wise.
signature_dishes: Breaded Hermelin cheese with berry-thyme sauce

km-eat-3.name: Soplicowo
km-eat-3.description: An old-Polish manor restaurant named for the Soplica estate in Mickiewicz's Pan Tadeusz, in the former palace of textile industrialist Wilhelm Teschemacher. The kitchen leans into old-nobility fare — roast duck and goose, game and offal done properly — with a cozy garden in warm weather. A go-to for weddings and family celebrations, so expect an occasion-ready feel.

km-eat-68.name: Pierogarnia Palce Lizać
km-eat-68.description: A homey, family-run pierogi spot on Milionowa, just south of Księży Młyn, that became locally famous after Magda Gessler's Kuchenne Rewolucje made it over. The owner later walked back the TV menu and returned to her own traditional cooking — pierogi made on-site and Silesian-dumpling comfort plates. Unpretentious and budget, a neighborhood pierogarnia rather than a design destination.
signature_dishes: Beef patties with Silesian dumplings (kluski śląskie)

km-eat-4.name: Cynamonowe Love — Bistro & Cafe
km-eat-4.cuisine: Bistro & cafe — breakfasts, brunch, waffles, coffee
km-eat-4.description: A cheerful, cinnamon-scented bistro and cafe on Piotrkowska near Geyer's White Factory — a red-brick textile-heritage neighbor to the Księży Młyn story (though just outside the district). Beloved for all-day breakfasts and both sweet and savory waffles, in a cosy room with genuinely warm service (Google ~4.8–4.9). A relaxed spot for brunch, matcha and a slow coffee.
signature_dishes: Sweet waffles (yogurt, chia, mango & passion fruit)

adds.name: Museum of Cinematography
adds.description: Poland's only museum devoted entirely to film history, in the opulent former palace of the Scheibler cotton dynasty at the old Water Market. Neo-Renaissance salons filled with antique projectors, magic lanterns and cinema posters — 19th-century factory-baron grandeur meets the story of the moving image in 'HollyŁódź'.
adds.history: Built 1855–1856 (attributed to Jan Karol Mertsching) for Karol Wilhelm Scheibler, Łódź's wealthiest industrialist. His widow Anna commissioned the lavish neo-Renaissance rebuild of 1884–1888 by Warsaw architect Edward Lilpop, with a Moorish palm house. Family seat until the 20th century; the Museum of Cinematography since 1 April 1986.
notable_facts: The only museum of its kind in Poland; open since 1 April 1986.
The neo-Renaissance rebuild was ordered by Scheibler's widow Anna, not Karol.
Anchors Łódź's UNESCO City of Film identity (home of the PWSFTviT film school).

adds.name: Herbst Palace Museum
adds.description: A jewel-box neo-Renaissance villa restored to the world of textile magnate Edward Herbst and his wife Matylda (née Scheibler). A branch of the Muzeum Sztuki — gilded salons, a mirror-lined ballroom, a landscaped garden and orangery, with a gallery of old-master and Polish painting in the former coach house.
adds.history: Built 1875–1877 as a wedding residence for Matylda, daughter of Karol Scheibler, and Edward Herbst, later a partner in the Scheibler empire; sited beside the mill so the master could watch the works. Attributed to city architect Hilary Majewski (probable). Revitalised 2011–2013 as a Muzeum Sztuki branch.
notable_facts: Europa Nostra award in 1990 for outstanding conservation.
The 2011–2013 restoration reconstructed the mirror ballroom and neo-baroque garden.
Matylda Herbst was Karol Scheibler's daughter — the palace ties into the dynasty.

adds.name: Scheibler's Spinning Mill
adds.description: The monumental, fortress-like red-brick spinning mill — roughly 207 m long — is the towering centrepiece of Księży Młyn and the most impressive industrial building in the 'Polish Manchester'. After cotton-spinning and postwar life as Uniontex, it reopened in 2010 as 'Lofty u Scheiblera', one of Poland's largest factory-to-apartment conversions.
adds.history: After buying the Księży Młyn lands in 1870, Karol Scheibler built a four-storey bare-brick spinning mill; the ~207 m building was completed in 1873 with ~70,000 spindles, the largest spinning works in Łódź. After the 1921 Scheibler–Grohman merger, part of interwar Poland's largest textile enterprise; under communism the Uniontex works. Converted to 400+ lofts 2005–2010 (opened 18 May 2010).
adds.architect: Mill designer not firmly attributed (1870s); loft conversion by Opal Property Developments
notable_facts: About 207 m long — the largest cotton-spinning building in Łódź; ~70,000 spindles at its peak.
The 2010 loft conversion (~400+ units) was the biggest factory-to-loft project in Poland.
Distinct from the nearby Fabryka Sztuki / Art_Inkubator (separate warehouses, Tymienieckiego 3).

adds.name: Book Art Museum (Henryk Grohman's Villa)
adds.description: A refined neo-Renaissance villa, home since 1993 to the Museum of Artistic Books — Poland's leading centre for hand-printed artist's books and bookbinding, in a working historic printing house. Built for Henryk Grohman, an art-patron whose music salon once heard Paderewski and Rubinstein at the organ.
adds.history: Designed by city architect Hilary Majewski in 1892–1893, initially as factory offices, it became the residence of Henryk Grohman, son of Ludwik and a noted collector. Remodelled 1903 (Chełmiński) and 1912 (Stebelski) with Viennese-Secession touches. Museum of Artistic Books since 1993.
notable_facts: Home of the Muzeum Książki Artystycznej (Book Art Museum) since 1993.
Its salon organ was reputedly played by Ignacy Paderewski and Artur Rubinstein.
Registered monument A/362 (15 Dec 1995).

adds.name: Ludwik Grohman's Villa
adds.description: A grand Italian-Renaissance residence built for Ludwik Grohman, whose family firm was Scheibler's great cotton partner (the empires merged in 1921). Restored by a private investor; its former garden survives as Kiliński Park.
adds.history: Built from 1881 to a design by city architect Hilary Majewski in an Italian-Renaissance idiom, enlarged 1894 after his son Leon's wedding with a grand staircase and winter garden. The Grohmans, from Saxony in the 1840s, were among Łódź's leading manufacturers and Scheibler's partners.
notable_facts: Interiors had a concert-hall/ballroom with original chandeliers and Berlin-made elevators.
Its former garden is now the public J. Kiliński Park.
A filming location for Marczewski's 1990 'Escape from the Liberty Cinema'.
Registered monument A/99 (20 Jan 1971).

adds.name: Church of St. Anne
adds.description: A compact neo-Romanesque brick church serving Księży Młyn, its 26-metre copper-clad tower a landmark on the edge of the factory quarter. The Herbst family funded the tower and bells in memory of their young daughter Anna, the parish's namesake.
adds.history: Cornerstone blessed 24 May 1904; land, brick and lime donated by mill owner Józef Meisner, plans by engineer Paweł Rübensham. Consecrated 10 December 1905. The Herbsts funded the tower, three bells, clock, choir stairs and mosaic floor in memory of their late daughter Anna.
notable_facts: Single-nave church of ~640 m² in pressed brick; copper-clad tower ~26 m high.
The Herbst family financed the tower, bells, clock and mosaic floor in memory of their daughter Anna.
Land and materials gifted by industrialist Józef Meisner.

adds.name: The Famuły — Workers' Housing Estate
adds.address: ul. Księży Młyn / Fabryczna / Przędzalniana, Łódź
adds.description: The long, rhythmic rows of two- and three-storey red-brick tenements — the famuły — that Scheibler built for his workforce, one of Europe's best-preserved 19th-century company towns. Along cobbled ul. Księży Młyn lies a self-contained world: identical brick barracks, a former school, shop, hospital and cultural hall.
adds.history: From the early 1870s Scheibler laid out a planned settlement of some forty brick famuły beside his mill. Conceived as self-sufficient — a factory school, company shops, a hospital and a cultural hall — an early paternalistic 'garden-city' model. About 25 estate houses hold ~300 apartments.
adds.architect: Not individually attributed (Scheibler works management; Majewski era — unconfirmed)
adds.architectural_style: Utilitarian red-brick industrial vernacular; planned settlement
notable_facts: About forty famuły built; mostly two- and three-storey brick blocks.
A complete 'city within a city' — housing, school, hospital, shops on-site.
One of the best-preserved worker settlements in Europe; a frequent period film backdrop.

adds.name: Źródliska Park & Palm House
adds.name_pl: Park Źródliska (I i II) / Park nad Jasieniem
adds.description: The oldest public park in Łódź, a shaded English-landscape garden on the springs of the Jasień beside the Scheibler palace. Its northern part shelters a glass Palm House full of exotics — a green counterpoint to the red-brick industry, and the very ground from which Scheibler carved his estate.
adds.history: Laid out in 1840 as the English Garden, arranged to an 1843 design by an engineer named Brochocki; the city's only municipal park until 1875. Around the late 1850s its western half (today Park Źródliska II) was sold to Scheibler, adjoining his palace and Moorish palm house. Fed by the springs of the Jasień, on which five mills once stood.
notable_facts: The oldest park in Łódź; its only municipal park until 1875.
Holds a Palm House (Palmiarnia) of exotic plants from old manufacturers' collections.
A registered heritage component of the Księży Młyn ensemble.
